result:
**Sampler** — a clockwork mouse bastes a hem across the bottom of the glass, one zigzag stitch per second, and on the minute a flying needle rips that hem out and re-uses the recovered thread to embroider the new numeral.

The time *is* the needlework. Minutes are satin-stitched: each numeral is a centre-line laid as a run of perpendicular threads, so a half-worked stroke simply stops where the needle is and the grain of the floss is visible. Hours are cross-stitched on a 3 px grid, one X per cell — a quieter grey weave, a slower technique for a slower unit. No colon. The sixty hem stitches are the only seconds hand, and when the sixtieth is in, the mouse has walked the whole width of the cloth.

The turn is one needle's itinerary. It rides the stitch frontier backwards to draw the old digit out (right to left), the mouse braces and hauls the hem apart, the slack arcs up across the face as a dotted sagging strand, and the needle runs forward again laying the new digit (left to right). The hour is the same performance, 6.5 s instead of 1.4, bracketed by the cross-stitch being picked out X by X and worked back in.

`node tools/check.mjs --design automaton-opus5` → **PASS**. 20160 frames, worst frame 0.82 ms / 1024 B (bus allows 1213 fps), 15.6 % of the glass lit on average, hottest pixel (29, 59) at 22.6 h/day, ~2.5 years to 50 % at full contrast.

Five rounds of fix-and-look got here. The ones that mattered: satin had to become discrete perpendicular bars (a continuous zigzag was spiky mush); the cross-stitch cell had to drop from 4 px to 3 px before 2, 4, 5, 8 and 9 read as digits; the haul thread had to become dotted and slack across its whole span, because a straight XOR line 90 px long reads as a laser; and the mouse needed a neck notch and a blunt rump — without them a 26x13 silhouette reads as a fish.

Honest weakest point: for about 0.15 s at a both-digits-change minute (:x9 → :x0, six times an hour) there is no minute on the cloth at all — only the hour, the mouse and the thread in flight. That gap is structural rather than sloppy: holding one old digit whole beside one new one would briefly display a wrong time, so the minute has to be fully off the cloth at the crossover. I shrank it from ~0.45 s to ~0.15 s with asymmetric easing (the last digit out clings on, the first one in arrives fast) but I could not close it without lying about the time. Second weakest: at the very start of each minute the mouse is pressed against the left edge and its tail trails off the glass.
